title: Biota, Environment and Conservation

toc.title: 14.1 Animal behaviour: reflex actions, taxes and migration
14.2 Air, water and soil pollution; pesticides
14.4 Conservation biology: biodiversity, protected areas, hotspots, Ramsar sites, IUCN categories and endangered species of Nepal

html:
This unit is rated at 2 questions in this book's estimate of the 40-question Zoology paper. It joins four compact topic blocks: how animals respond and move, how pollution moves through air/water/soil and food chains, how body design fits water/land/air, and how conservation status is assigned. Nepal-specific examples—Chitwan, Koshi Tappu, rhino/tiger recovery, red panda and Ramsar wetlands—are especially valuable.

What the paper asks from this chapter
  • Taxis is directed whole-body movement toward/away from a stimulus; kinesis is an undirected change in speed/turning; a reflex is a rapid response through a reflex arc.
  • Migration is regular, usually seasonal two-way movement. Salmon are anadromous (sea → river to breed); eels are catadromous (river → sea).
  • Air: SO₂/NOₓ → acid rain; CFC chlorine → stratospheric ozone loss; CO₂/CH₄/N₂O → enhanced greenhouse effect. These are three different mechanisms.
  • Water pollution chain: nutrients/organic waste → algal/microbial growth → BOD rises → dissolved oxygen falls → fish die.
  • Persistent fat-soluble pesticides bioaccumulate in an individual and biomagnify across trophic levels.
  • Flight signature: feathers/wings, pneumatic bones, keeled sternum, huge pectorals, air sacs and weight-saving anatomy.
  • IUCN order: EX, EW, CR, EN, VU, NT, LC; CR+EN+VU are “threatened”. Nepal examples: rhino/snow leopard VU; tiger/red panda EN; gharial/pangolin CR.

14.1 Animal behaviour: reflex actions, taxes and migration

Behaviour is an animal's observable response to internal or external stimuli. Its scientific study is ethology. Innate behaviour is inherited and stereotyped; learned behaviour is modified by experience. Most real behaviour combines genetic predisposition with learning.

Reflexes, taxes and kineses

A reflex action is a rapid, involuntary and stereotyped response mediated by a reflex arc:

receptor → sensory neuron → CNS → motor neuron → effector

Withdrawal from a hot object, blinking and the knee jerk are examples. A reflex usually moves only part of the body and is fast because the pathway is short.

A taxis (plural taxes) is directed locomotion of the whole organism relative to a stimulus. Movement toward it is positive and away from it is negative:

Taxis Stimulus Example
Phototaxis light moth toward a lamp; cockroach away from light
Chemotaxis chemical mosquito toward CO₂/body odours; sperm toward egg signals
Geotaxis gravity many soil invertebrates move downward
Rheotaxis water current fish orient/swim against current
Thermotaxis temperature animals move toward a preferred temperature
Thigmotaxis touch/contact cockroaches keep contact with walls/crevices

A kinesis is undirected: stimulus intensity changes speed or turning rate, but the animal does not steer toward a source. Woodlice move and turn more in dry air and less in humid air, so they accumulate in damp places by differential activity rather than navigation.

A fixed action pattern is a more complex innate sequence released by a sign stimulus and usually carried to completion, such as egg-retrieval in geese. Instinct is a broader inherited programme such as web spinning or nest building. Habituation, conditioning, imitation and insight are forms of learning.

Migration

Migration is regular, often seasonal, two-way movement between breeding and non-breeding/feeding areas. It tracks food, water, climate and breeding sites, at the cost of energy and exposure to predators. Birds may migrate latitudinally or altitudinally; bar-headed geese and demoiselle cranes cross or pass through the Himalayan region. Animals navigate using the sun, stars, polarised light, landmarks, odours and sensitivity to Earth's magnetic field, with an internal clock correcting for time.

Fish terminology is a frequent trap:

  • Anadromous: adults live mainly at sea and migrate into fresh water to spawn—salmon.
  • Catadromous: adults live mainly in fresh water and migrate to the sea to spawn—freshwater eels.
  • Potamodromous: migration entirely within fresh water.
  • Oceanodromous: migration entirely within the sea.
Worked example — taxis, kinesis or reflex?

Classify three observations: (i) a moth flies towards a lamp; (ii) woodlice move faster in dry air and settle when they reach damp air, with no set direction; (iii) a finger is jerked off a hot pan before any pain is felt.

  • (i) Positive phototaxis — locomotion directed towards the light stimulus.
  • (ii) Kinesis — the rate of movement changes with humidity but direction is random; the animals simply accumulate where movement slows.
  • (iii) A reflex — a fixed, involuntary, spinal response; the conscious pain registers slightly later.

The deciding test: is the movement aimed at/away from the stimulus (taxis), merely faster or slower (kinesis), or an automatic neural arc (reflex)?

Trap — biomagnification is about concentration, not amount eaten

A persistent pollutant such as DDT becomes more concentrated at each higher trophic level (water → plankton → small fish → large fish → bird) because it is fat-soluble and neither excreted nor broken down; the famous end-result is thin-shelled eggs in birds of prey. It is different from eutrophication (nutrient enrichment → algal bloom → oxygen crash) — MCQs like to blur the two.

Mark–recapture: counting animals you cannot line up

Problem. In a Chitwan grassland, 40 spotted deer are captured, marked and released. Weeks later 50 are captured, and 10 of them carry marks. Estimate the population. A second survey marks 60, recaptures 80, finds 12 marked — what estimate now? Solution. Lincoln–Petersen: N = (marked first × captured second) ÷ recaptured marked = (40 × 50) ÷ 10 = 200 deer. Second survey: (60 × 80) ÷ 12 = 400. The method assumes marks neither help nor hurt survival and that mixing is complete — break either assumption and the estimate lies, which is why real censuses repeat the capture many times over.

14.2 Air, water and soil pollution; pesticides

Pollution is an undesirable change in the physical, chemical or biological characteristics of air, water or soil that harms organisms, ecosystems or human use. A pollutant may be primary (emitted in harmful form, such as CO or SO₂) or secondary (formed in the environment, such as tropospheric ozone, PAN or acid-rain acids). Sources may be point (a factory pipe) or non-point (fertiliser/pesticide run-off from many fields).

Air pollution

Pollutant/process Source and effect
Particulate matter (PM₂.₅/PM₁₀) combustion, dust, brick kilns; penetrates airways/alveoli, aggravates respiratory and cardiovascular disease
Carbon monoxide incomplete combustion; binds haemoglobin much more strongly than O₂, reducing oxygen delivery
SO₂ and NOₓ fossil fuels/vehicles/industry; respiratory irritation and conversion to sulphuric/nitric acids
Acid rain precipitation below the natural pH of about 5.6; acidifies lakes/soils, mobilises toxic aluminium, damages leaves/buildings
Ground-level ozone/PAN secondary products of NOₓ + volatile organics in sunlight (photochemical smog); injure lungs and crops
CFCs old refrigerants/aerosols; UV releases chlorine that catalytically destroys stratospheric ozone
Greenhouse gases CO₂, CH₄, N₂O and fluorinated gases absorb outgoing infrared, enhancing warming

Do not merge the three atmospheric problems: greenhouse gases warm by trapping outgoing infrared mainly in the troposphere; ozone depletion admits more incoming UV through the stratosphere; acid rain is wet/dry deposition of acids formed from SO₂ and NOₓ.

Water pollution and eutrophication

Sewage, industrial effluents, fertiliser/pesticide run-off, oil, heated water, plastics and pathogens pollute water. Eutrophication follows nutrient enrichment, especially nitrogen and phosphorus:

nutrients → algal/cyanobacterial bloom → light blocked and plants die → decomposition increases BOD → dissolved O₂ crashes → fish/invertebrates die

Clean water has low BOD and high dissolved oxygen. Heavy metals such as lead, cadmium, chromium and mercury do not “rot away”; they persist, bind proteins and may enter food chains. Excess nitrate in drinking water and geogenic arsenic/fluoride are chemical hazards distinct from microbial contamination.

Soil pollution and pesticides

Soil is polluted by excessive fertiliser/pesticide, industrial sludge, mine waste, leaking fuel, plastics and unsegregated municipal waste. Consequences include loss of soil microbiota/earthworms, nutrient imbalance, salinity, groundwater leaching and uptake of toxins by crops.

A pesticide is used against a pest group—such as insecticides, herbicides, fungicides or rodenticides. Its environmental behaviour matters as much as its immediate kill:

  • Organochlorines such as DDT are persistent and fat-soluble, making them prone to bioaccumulation/biomagnification.
  • Organophosphates/carbamates inhibit acetylcholinesterase; generally less persistent but can be acutely toxic.
  • Pyrethroids alter nerve sodium channels and can be highly toxic to fish and aquatic invertebrates.
  • Neonicotinoids are systemic neuroactive insecticides of concern for pollinators and aquatic insects.

Bioaccumulation is build-up within one organism over time. Biomagnification is rising concentration at successive trophic levels because predators consume many contaminated prey while retaining most of the persistent chemical.

Integrated pest management combines monitoring/thresholds, crop rotation and resistant varieties, habitat for natural enemies, biocontrol/mechanical methods and targeted chemicals only when needed, reducing resistance and non-target damage.

14.3 Aquatic, terrestrial and volant adaptations

An adaptation is an inherited morphological, physiological or behavioural trait shaped by natural selection that improves survival/reproduction in a particular environment. It differs from acclimatisation, a reversible adjustment within an individual's lifetime.

Aquatic adaptations

Water is dense, buoyant, thermally buffering and oxygen-poor compared with air. Typical fish solutions are:

  • fusiform/streamlined body, backward-pointing scales and mucus to reduce drag;
  • caudal fin for thrust, dorsal/anal fins against rolling and paired fins for steering/braking;
  • large, thin gill lamellae with counter-current blood/water flow;
  • a swim bladder for neutral buoyancy in many bony fishes;
  • lateral-line detection of vibration/current and often countershading.

Osmoregulation reverses between media. A freshwater bony fish gains water and loses salts, so it excretes abundant dilute urine and actively absorbs ions at the gills. A marine bony fish loses water to the sea, drinks seawater, excretes excess salt at the gills and produces scant urine. Secondary aquatic mammals such as dolphins breathe air with lungs and use flippers/blubber; they are not fish despite a convergent outline.

Terrestrial adaptations

Land removes buoyant support and creates desiccation and temperature stress. Terrestrial animals evolve strong limbs/skeletons, waterproof skin or cuticle, internal lungs/tracheae, water-conserving excretory products and internal fertilisation or shelled eggs. By locomotor habit:

Habit Design Examples
Cursorial (running) long limbs, reduced digits, digitigrade/unguligrade stance, elastic tendons horse, chital, blackbuck
Arboreal (trees) grasping/opposable digits, claws or adhesive pads, prehensile tail in some, binocular vision langur, red panda, many geckos
Fossorial (burrowing) compact/spindle body, strong forelimbs/claws, reduced eyes/external ears mole, pangolin
Desert/xeric nocturnality, burrows, concentrated urine/dry faeces, metabolic water, heat tolerance camel, kangaroo rat
Cold/high-altitude insulation, compact extremities, counter-current limb heat exchange, high oxygen-carrying capacity yak, snow leopard, marmot

Bergmann's rule predicts larger body size in colder populations of related endotherms; Allen's rule predicts shorter appendages in cold climates. Both reduce surface-area-to-volume heat loss and are tendencies, not laws.

Volant (flight) adaptations

True powered flight evolved independently in insects, birds and bats (and in extinct pterosaurs). In birds, the examination list is:

  • streamlined body and feathers forming smooth aerofoils;
  • forelimbs transformed into wings with fused/reduced hand bones;
  • pneumatic bones that are hollow but internally strutted;
  • a deep keeled sternum (carina) anchoring huge pectoral flight muscles;
  • air sacs connected to lungs, supporting highly efficient, largely one-way airflow and cooling;
  • four-chambered heart/double circulation and high metabolic rate;
  • weight economy: beak instead of teeth/jaw heaviness, no urinary bladder, semi-solid uric-acid excretion and compact reproductive organs outside the breeding season.

Bats instead fly on a skin patagium stretched over greatly elongated finger bones. Gliders such as flying squirrels descend on membranes but do not sustain powered flapping flight.

14.4 Conservation biology: biodiversity, protected areas, hotspots, Ramsar sites, IUCN categories and endangered species of Nepal

Biodiversity is variety at genetic, species and ecosystem levels. Species diversity has both richness (how many species) and evenness (how equally abundant they are). A major threat mnemonic is HIPPO: Habitat loss, Invasive species, Pollution, Population/consumption pressure and Overexploitation—now all amplified by climate change.

Measuring evenness with Simpson's index

A sample contains four species with counts 50, 25, 15 and 10, so N=100. Simpson's dominance is

D=\frac{\sum n_i(n_i-1)}{N(N-1)} =\frac{50(49)+25(24)+15(14)+10(9)}{100(99)} =\frac{3350}{9900}=0.338

Simpson's diversity is 1-D=0.662, and the reciprocal 1/D=2.96 is the effective number of equally common species. It is below the richness of 4 because one species dominates.

In-situ and ex-situ conservation; protected areas

In-situ conservation protects a species in its natural ecosystem—national parks, wildlife reserves, conservation areas, buffer zones/community forests— so ecological interactions and natural selection continue. Ex-situ conservation protects components outside the habitat—zoos, botanical gardens, seed/gene banks, cryopreservation and captive breeding. Ex-situ methods are insurance and a source for reintroduction; they do not by themselves replace a functioning wild ecosystem.

Nepal's network under the National Parks and Wildlife Conservation Act is described in current departmental summaries as 13 national parks, one wildlife reserve, one hunting reserve and seven conservation areas, in addition to buffer zones. Management categories differ:

Category Nepal example Defining management
National park Chitwan (first, 1973); Sagarmatha; Bardiya strict ecosystem protection; resource extraction/hunting prohibited
Wildlife reserve Koshi Tappu (only one) protection of particular species/habitats, especially arna and wetland birds
Hunting reserve Dhorpatan (only one) tightly licensed, quota-based trophy hunting
Conservation area Annapurna (largest); Kanchenjunga; Manaslu multiple use with resident communities participating in management
Buffer zone around Chitwan/Bardiya and other parks regulated use and revenue-sharing to build local support/reduce conflict

Biodiversity hotspots and Ramsar sites

A Conservation International biodiversity hotspot must contain at least 1,500 endemic vascular plant species and have lost at least 70% of its original habitat. Nepal's mountain and foothill ecosystems form part of the Himalaya hotspot, one reason the country holds exceptional species richness over a steep elevation gradient.

Ramsar sites are wetlands of international importance designated under the Ramsar Convention (Iran, 1971). Nepal has ten: Koshi Tappu, Beeshazari and associated lakes, Ghodaghodi Lake area, Jagadishpur Reservoir, Gokyo and associated lakes, Gosaikunda and associated lakes, Phoksundo Lake, Rara Lake, Mai Pokhari and the Lake Cluster of Pokhara Valley. Ramsar designation is a commitment to “wise use”, not automatically the same legal category as a national park.

IUCN categories and threatened animals of Nepal

The IUCN Red List orders evaluated species as:

EX Extinct → EW Extinct in the Wild → CR Critically Endangered → EN Endangered → VU Vulnerable → NT Near Threatened → LC Least Concern

DD (Data Deficient) and NE (Not Evaluated) sit outside that risk ranking. A species is threatened only if it is CR, EN or VU. Status is quantitative and can change after reassessment; “endangered” in ordinary speech is not the same as the formal EN category.

Nepal animal Scientific name Global IUCN status used here
Gharial Gavialis gangeticus Critically Endangered
Chinese pangolin Manis pentadactyla Critically Endangered
White-rumped vulture Gyps bengalensis Critically Endangered
Bengal florican Houbaropsis bengalensis Critically Endangered
Bengal tiger Panthera tigris Endangered
Red panda Ailurus fulgens Endangered
Asian elephant Elephas maximus Endangered
Wild water buffalo (arna) Bubalus arnee Endangered
Himalayan musk deer Moschus leucogaster Endangered
Greater one-horned rhinoceros Rhinoceros unicornis Vulnerable
Snow leopard Panthera uncia Vulnerable
Swamp deer Rucervus duvaucelii Vulnerable

Anti-poaching protection, habitat management, biological corridors, buffer-zone benefit sharing and translocation have produced documented recoveries of two flagship mammals. Their increase also creates new management duties: prey and habitat carrying capacity, genetic mixing and prevention/compensation of human–wildlife conflict.

The collapse of South Asian Gyps vultures shows the opposite lesson: veterinary diclofenac left in cattle carcasses caused renal failure in feeding vultures. Banning veterinary diclofenac, promoting safer meloxicam, captive breeding and drug-free vulture feeding sites converted an invisible chemical threat into a manageable conservation problem.

Common mistake

Four pairs the paper swaps: taxis is directed, kinesis is not (a moth steering to light vs a woodlouse merely slowing in damp); bioaccumulation is build-up within one body, biomagnification is the climb up the food chain; a national park excludes human use strictly, a conservation area is managed with the communities inside it; CR (critically endangered) is one step from the wild's edge, EN (endangered) one step behind CR — 'endangered' in headlines often means the whole CR+EN+VU 'threatened' club.

Formula and fact sheet

  • Reflex = receptor → sensory neuron → CNS → motor neuron → effector.
  • Taxis = directed whole-organism orientation; kinesis = undirected rate change.
  • Anadromous = sea to river; catadromous = river to sea.
  • SO₂/NOₓ → acid rain; CFC-Cl → stratospheric ozone depletion; greenhouse gases → infrared trapping.
  • Eutrophication: nutrient ↑ → bloom ↑ → decomposition/BOD ↑ → dissolved O₂ ↓.
  • Bioaccumulation is within an organism; biomagnification is across trophic levels.
  • Freshwater fish: water in, dilute urine out, salts absorbed. Marine bony fish: drinks, salt excreted at gills, scant urine.
  • Cursorial = running; arboreal = trees; fossorial = burrowing; volant = flying.
  • Bird flight: feathers, pneumatic bones, keeled sternum, pectorals, air sacs.
  • Simpson diversity =1-D, where D=\sum n_i(n_i-1)/[N(N-1)]; 1/D = effective species number.
  • Ramsar = wetlands of international importance; Nepal has 10 listed sites.
  • IUCN: EX, EW, CR, EN, VU, NT, LC; threatened = CR+EN+VU.

Rapid-revision tables and high-yield facts

Quantity Value
Reflex arc receptor → sensory → interneuron → motor → effector
Taxis vs kinesis directed vs undirected activity change
Migration cues sun, stars, magnetic field, smell, landmarks
Acid rain pH < 5.6 (H₂SO₄, HNO₃)
Montreal Protocol 1987, CFC phase-out
DDT magnification 0.000003 ppm water → 25 ppm fish-eating birds (≈8 million ×)
Lincoln–Petersen N = M·C ÷ R
IUCN threatened club CR + EN + VU
Nepal protected areas 12 NP + 1 WR + 6 CA + 1 HR ≈ 23 % of land
Ramsar 10 sites; Koshi Tappu first, 1987
Census rhino 752 (2021), tiger 355 (2022)
Nepal symbols monal = national bird; spiny babbler endemic

Chapter summary

  • Reflexes, taxes and kineses differ by pathway, body involvement and whether movement is directed.
  • Migration trades travel costs for seasonal access to food and breeding habitat and relies on multiple navigational cues.
  • Air pollution separates into particles/toxic gases, smog, acid deposition, ozone depletion and greenhouse warming.
  • Water and soil pollutants may be biodegradable, nutrient-like or persistent; persistence plus fat solubility creates biomagnification.
  • Aquatic and terrestrial animals solve opposite mechanical/osmotic problems, while flight imposes the strictest combined demands for lift, power and low mass.
  • Biodiversity includes genes, species and ecosystems, and evenness matters as well as species count.
  • In-situ protected areas preserve whole systems; ex-situ collections are a complementary safety net.
  • Hotspots and Ramsar sites prioritise exceptional endemic-rich and wetland ecosystems under threat.
  • IUCN categories make extinction risk comparable, and Nepal's rhino, tiger and vulture programmes show that specific threat removal can work.

Answers and explanations — Set A

1. (b) — The arc runs receptor → afferent → CNS → efferent → effector.

2. (d) — Positive taxis is oriented toward the stimulus.

3. (c) — Chemotaxis is direction relative to a chemical gradient.

4. (a) — Kinesis changes activity/turning without steering to a source.

5. (c) — Anadromous fishes ascend rivers from the sea to spawn.

6. (d) — CO and SO₂ are emitted directly; ozone/PAN/acids are secondary products.

7. (c) — SO₂ and NOₓ oxidise to sulphuric and nitric acids.

8. (d) — UV photolysis of CFCs releases ozone-destroying chlorine atoms.

9. (a) — Methane is emitted by ruminants, wetlands, rice fields and waste.

10. (b) — Nitrogen and phosphorus commonly limit and then fertilise aquatic production.

11. (b) — Concentration rises from prey to predator across a food chain.

12. (d) — DDT is a persistent organochlorine insecticide.

13. (c) — Gas volume in the swim bladder adjusts overall density.

14. (b) — Neuromasts detect pressure waves, currents and nearby movement.

15. (b) — Cursorial animals are running specialists.

16. (a) — Fossorial means adapted for digging/burrowing.

17. (a) — Pneumatic bones reduce mass while retaining strutted strength.

18. (d) — The carina anchors the large downstroke/upstroke flight muscles.

19. (d) — Short appendages reduce exposed surface and heat loss.

20. (b) — The three standard levels are genetic, species and ecosystem diversity.

21. (c) — A national park protects organisms within their ecosystem.

22. (a) — Gene/seed banks conserve material outside the natural habitat.

23. (c) — Critically Endangered, Endangered and Vulnerable are the threatened classes.

24. (d) — Ramsar sites are wetlands of international importance.

25. (a) — Recovery has placed the greater one-horned rhino in VU, not EN.

Answers and explanations — Set B

1. (a) — Directional orientation is the defining distinction.

2. (d) — Spinal integration launches withdrawal before cortical pain perception completes.

3. (a) — Seasonal resource tracking outweighs travel costs in reproductive success.

4. (c) — Tropospheric ozone is a photochemical product, not mainly a direct emission.

5. (d) — The two processes involve different atmospheric layers and wavelengths.

6. (c) — Microbial oxidation lowers dissolved oxygen below aquatic animals' needs.

7. (b) — Each predator integrates the retained burden of many prey.

8. (d) — Freshwater fish replace urinary/diffusive salt losses by gill uptake.

9. (c) — Air-sac ventilation sustains gas exchange and heat loss during flight.

10. (a) — Long loops of Henle and behaviour minimise water loss; oxidation supplies metabolic water.

11. (b) — Equal richness can conceal very unequal abundances.

12. (b) — Small isolated fragments suffer edge exposure, drift/inbreeding and loss of dispersal.

13. (c) — A zoo/gene bank cannot by itself maintain pollinators, prey, migration and selection.

14. (b) — Benefits align local livelihoods with wildlife protection.

15. (a) — Hotspot priority is irreplaceability plus extreme habitat loss.
